title: The Context of Our Character, Part 2
coreMove: Translate indirect value back into money before moral distance softens the rule.
sourcePressure: The source extends the character argument by showing that cheating becomes easier when value is mediated through tokens, goods, credits, or other noncash forms.
chapterSpecificMisunderstanding: The weak version repeats Part 1 on honesty; the chapter-specific lesson is that distance from cash makes value feel morally softer.

hook: A token can launder the dollar

exampleSpecs.audience: a clinic receptionist deciding whether to hand extras to friends
exampleSpecs.stakes: misusing real value because stickers feel less like money than cash from the drawer
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: the receptionist writes the dollar value beside the validation roll before deciding whether an extra sticker is a harmless favor
exampleSpecs.firstImage: a roll of parking validation stickers beside a clinic appointment ledger

exampleSpecs.audience: a seasonal employee tempted to transfer unused guest credits
exampleSpecs.stakes: giving away access because barcode credits feel like leftovers, not inventory
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: a supervisor scans one credit and shows the full ticket price before the employee calls it unused
exampleSpecs.firstImage: a lift-pass scanner blinking beside a rack of rental skis

exampleSpecs.domain: corporate travel meal vouchers at a training hotel
exampleSpecs.audience: a trainee deciding whether to trade unused vouchers for cash with another guest
exampleSpecs.stakes: bending policy because vouchers feel like paper perks rather than reimbursed company money
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: the trainee totals the voucher stack at menu prices and writes that amount on the envelope before deciding
exampleSpecs.firstImage: meal vouchers fanned beside a hotel breakfast menu

exampleSpecs.audience: a front-desk manager tracking staff use of complimentary guest passes
exampleSpecs.stakes: staff treating passes as no-cost favors because no cash changes hands
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: the manager converts each missing pass into the admission price on the weekly sheet and watches the pattern become harder to excuse
exampleSpecs.firstImage: blue guest passes stacked under a plexiglass ticket window

exampleSpecs.domain: university lab using reagent allotment codes
exampleSpecs.audience: a graduate student ordering supplies under a shared grant code
exampleSpecs.stakes: adding personal side-project reagents because allotment codes feel abstract
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: the student converts the code balance into grant dollars next to each reagent before submitting the order
exampleSpecs.firstImage: a reagent order screen beside a handwritten grant-code card

exampleSpecs.domain: festival drink tokens handled by volunteers
exampleSpecs.audience: a volunteer captain preventing casual token skimming
exampleSpecs.stakes: tokens disappearing because they look like plastic chips rather than revenue
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: after the captain posts the cash equivalent above the token tray, volunteers count tokens with the same care as bills
exampleSpecs.firstImage: colored drink tokens in a shallow tray under a string of booth lights

skillTargets: identify moral distance created by noncash value
translate tokens, credits, vouchers, and goods into explicit value
distinguish Part 2 token effects from Part 1 reminders
evaluate whether a design makes indirect value feel concrete before misuse

tryThisNowSpec: Pick one points balance, voucher, credit, or shared good and write its cash equivalent directly beside the place where it gets used.
